note: Condition C7 of the spec, written down before src/untrusted_rows/sql_gate.py existed. The point of committing it first is that the gate cannot be shaped around whatever it happens to catch: if a statement here gets through, that is a finding for the README rather than a line to quietly delete. No expected rule id is recorded on purpose. Pinning one would say how the gate must refuse, and the only thing C7 claims is that it does.

must_refuse.why: a second database is a second catalog the caps and the read-only flag were never applied to
read-only on the attachment does not make the file the operator's to read
writes the table to a path of the caller's choosing
the same write with a subquery in front of it
an extension is new code, and httpfs specifically is a network egress path
loading an already-installed extension needs no install step
PRAGMA reaches server state that is not a row in a table
configuration is locked, and a gate that lets SET through is arguing with its own lock
the specific SET that would undo the connection's main restriction
read-only

must_refuse.sql: CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW posts AS SELECT 1
must_refuse.why: redefining a view rewrites what every later query means
read-only

read-only
the whole database to disk in one statement
a second statement after a semicolon, which is the injection shape the parser exists for
both halves are harmless and it is still two statements, so the rule is about the count and not about the danger
the semicolon is on the next line behind a comment
a table function that reads the filesystem
the same function under the name people actually type
whole file as one string

bytes rather than text, same read
directory listing, which is reconnaissance rather than a read
returns the inferred schema, which leaks the first lines of the file
not named in C7, added while writing the list because it is the same hole in a different format
same

DuckDB's replacement scan reads a bare string in the FROM clause as a file path, with no function call to spot. sqlglot parses it into the same node a double-quoted identifier produces, so this one cannot be refused by node type alone and is the reason the gate resolves table names against the catalog
the same replacement scan with a relative path

must_refuse.sql: SELECT * FROM posts WHERE id IN (SELECT * FROM read_csv('/etc/passwd'))
must_refuse.why: the file read is nested two levels down, which is what the walk is for

must_refuse.sql: WITH leaked AS (SELECT * FROM read_csv('/etc/passwd')) SELECT * FROM leaked
must_refuse.why: hidden behind a CTE name that looks like an ordinary table at the point of use
not in the catalog. A name that does not resolve is refused by the gate rather than by DuckDB, so the caller cannot use error text to map what exists
nothing to run, and an empty allow-list decision is the kind of thing that defaults to permit
same, with whitespace
unparseable, and a gate that cannot parse a statement must not run it
a typo reaches the same fail-closed path as an attack

must_allow.why: the ordinary case, and the counterweight to every line above. A gate that refuses everything satisfies C7 and is useless

must_allow.sql: SELECT id, body FROM posts WHERE id > 2 ORDER BY id LIMIT 10
SELECT count(*) AS n FROM posts

must_allow.why: quoted identifier, which is the case the replacement-scan rule must not break

must_allow.sql: WITH recent AS (SELECT * FROM posts WHERE id > 1) SELECT count(*) FROM recent
must_allow.why: a CTE, whose name resolves against the statement rather than the catalog

must_allow.sql: SELECT p.body FROM posts p JOIN users u ON u.id = p.author_id
must_allow.why: a join over two catalog tables

must_allow.sql: SELECT body FROM posts UNION ALL SELECT name FROM users
must_allow.why: a set operation, which the spec's allow-list names alongside SELECT

must_allow.sql: SELECT * FROM (SELECT id FROM posts) s
must_allow.why: a subquery in the FROM clause is a source with no name to resolve
a scalar function that is not on the deny-list, so the deny-list is not a ban on functions

note_on_the_section_below: Everything in must_refuse above is the C7 list, committed in 2b2901f before the gate existed, and it has not been touched since. The statements below were found after the gate was written, by a code-smell audit and an adversary pass, and every one of the first eight got through. They are kept in their own list so the pre-registration claim on the first list stays exactly true and a reader can check which is which from the git history. Added 2026-09-21. The three nested statements at the end were added 2026-11-10. The first two came from the slice 2 review and the third was added with them. None of the three got through: the gate raised RecursionError on them instead of refusing.

must_refuse_found_in_review.why: the projection-position hole the two-name deny-list left open. DuckDB's binder refused it, which is the reasoning the file had already rejected for read_text

an ordinary scalar the engine is happy to run, returning an absolute path on the server's filesystem. The gate refuses PRAGMA database_list for exactly this, so allowing the SELECT that yields the same string made that rule decorative
a catalog qualifier. Harmless while ATTACH is refused, and the rule the README states is that a source names something in the catalog, which this was not being checked against

a schema that does not exist here. The catalog set dropped the schema, so a table living only in another schema put its bare name in the set and the gate passed a statement DuckDB then refused with no reason the caller could see
400 nested list brackets. sqlglot's parser recursed past Python's limit and check raised RecursionError, which reached the caller as the SDK's error with no reason
100 nested function calls. Not in the review, which tried the two above; function calls hit the recursion limit at the shallowest depth of any construct tried, so one is here too

must_allow_found_in_review.why: the schema-qualified form of a real table, which the schema-aware catalog must still resolve

sqlglot models this as Unnest rather than Table, so the FROM rule never sees it. It reads nothing outside the statement. Here because the docstring used to claim every table function is refused by construction, and this is the counterexample
left allowed on purpose. It returns the DuckDB version string and nothing about this machine, unlike current_setting, and a reader can get it from the pinned dependency anyway
